comments.text: 0:25 you are mistaken there, Mike. Luge, skeleton, and bobsleigh don’t run on blades. If they did, they’d be out of control the first turn they made. Instead, they slide on runners, cylindrical metal skids that don’t cut into the ice surface as much as run across it. You’ll often hear commentators refer to the bottom section of a run as “gliding,” because by that time, the runners have encountered enough friction to heat up slightly. That heat causes a tiny, almost molecularly thin layer of ice to melt against the runner, meaning the sled is gliding in a layer of water, which reduces friction and you’ll see the sleds REALLY pick up speed. But there are no blades on any sled… you are far more likely to break a bone or get friction burns than get cut

comments.text:
I was really hoping Petra Majdič would be included.

During the warm-up for the 1.4 km classic sprint on 17 February in the 2010 Olympics she skied off-course, down a bank, into a 3 m (10 ft) deep gully where she crashed on rocks breaking both ski poles, a ski tip, and sustained five broken ribs along with a pneumothorax.The start time for her qualifying round was pushed back, but she collapsed in pain after qualifying and was taken to hospital to be x-rayed. The ultrasound failed to show the rib fractures. Thus, she returned to the course and, despite the agonizing pain, won her quarterfinal and just got through the semifinal as a lucky loser. During the semifinal, one of the broken ribs pierced her lung, collapsing it. Despite this and the excruciating pain, she finished third to win the bronze medal in the final, the first individual Winter Olympic medal for Slovenia in 16 years. She earned the highest praise from other skiers, staff and the media for her amazing bravery as she attended the medal giving ceremony with a tube in her chest to relieve pneumothorax. She said at the press conference afterward "Today, this is not a bronze. This is a gold with little diamonds on it".
comments.author: @DomenBremecXCVI

comments.text:
2010, I’m 10 years old watching the Olympics with my family. Unable to sit still, I decide I too will attempt an Olympian feat of athleticism. Quietly retreating to a hallway doorway, I shimmy my way up the frame (iykyk). Head now touching the roof, I take a deep breath. 

This is it. 

This is the moment I’ve been training for. 

I throw myself forward into an astonishing double flip, wowing the crowds and landing with superhuman level control. I open my eyes. Head fully extended back, I’m eye level with the dust bunnies under the couch, chest to the floor. My chin is split open to the bone. I know because I can see it, after sneaking into the family bathroom. I hold a wad of toilet paper against the red and white, exposed structure. My twin sister is at the door. 

“Open up, I have to pee.”

“No.”

“Seriously, you’ve been in there forever.” 

“Fine. Only if you promise not to tell.”

“Sure.” 

…. Moments later, I’m rushed to the hospital where I receive a lovely goatee of stitches (just in time for my first day in private school, fourth grade). After all was said and done, I got a McDonald’s ice cream cone, the memory of staying up later than I ever had before, and a sick scar.
comments.author: @emilyrose7231

comments.text: I actually work with skaters and am a professional sharpener and skate repair man and laces are extremely important. Some figure skating boots are almost entirely designed around a specific lacing technique and way of support. Lace problems are actually common and some people don't even use laces, instead using mechanical closures like the BOA system, going so far as to counting exact number of clicks. Skaters will ship skates and pay absurd amounts of money to only have 1 person they trust work on their skates. I've had skaters drive 2 hours to meet me just for a simple sharpening.
comments.author: @TheGreatChrisB

comments.text:
9:46 
As an alpine skier, I can see that she got injured in her knee because her ski boot got swept under her and it would have rotated her flexed foot position to one side and then the other because ski boots are so stiff from toe to just below the knee. 
Unfortunately skis for the Olympics would have sharp skate-blade like edges. 
The skis popping off on impact is actually a safety feature because injuries can be so much worse if long adult size skis stay on during a fall. 
The ski equipment being all over the place around a person who fell, but who is ok, is what skiers call a yard sale or yard sail. 
(It could have either origin/meaning/reference in this context) 
In surfing this would probably be called a wipeout. 
As long as the person is ok, then it’s just a learning experience that people on the lift above can call a yard sale.
comments.author: @SeaOfSoapOperaLifeDrama

comments.text:
6:30 I have never supported at a figure skating event, but I have a lot of experiance working at football (soccer) and athletics competitions. No one is allowed on the field until the referee gives his ok. Often the referee does his first check on the athlete. Then the trainer or physiotherapist is allowed to enter. After they checked in with the athlete there is a quick talk between the referee and the trainer/physiotherapist. Only after that does the referee decide if they allow medics (together with the team doctor) on the field. The reason is for example a fear of doping mid game.

After the incident with Christian Eriksen in Copenhagen in 2021, the rules got a bit more lax, but they are still pretty strict. Now it is more like "Everything is the same, but if we see from the sides that the athlete is probably dead, we are allowed on the field without beeing released by the referee".
